explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. God says, “For six days work may be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of complete rest, a day of sacred assembly.” Then He adds, “You must not do any work; wherever you live, it is a Sabbath to the LORD.” That “wherever you live…” closes the door on the home-office loophole.

That's it, friend. “You must not do any work; wherever you live, it is a Sabbath to the LORD.” Whether the house is in the middle of the camp or off at the edge, it's the same rest. Not even one little email from the kitchen table.
Unleavened bread it is. God says, “For seven days you must eat unleavened bread.” Seven days, friend. As a cookie guy, I have questions about a week of that, but I just follow the instructions.

Barley is a fair guess, since bread has to come from somewhere. But the text doesn't name a grain for this feast. It names the kind of bread: “For seven days you must eat unleavened bread.” The word that matters is unleavened.
Honey sounds delicious, and my sweet tooth voted for it too. But the text never mentions honey here. God says, “For seven days you must eat unleavened bread.” That's the whole bread order.

True, friend. On the first day, “…you are to hold a sacred assembly; you are not to do any regular work.” The seventh day gets the same: “On the seventh day there shall be a sacred assembly; you must not do any regular work.” So the feast has a sacred assembly at each end.

This one is actually true, friend, so let's look again. The first day has a sacred assembly and no regular work. The seventh day has its own: “On the seventh day there shall be a sacred assembly; you must not do any regular work.” Same rule at both ends of the feast.

He waves it, friend. God says, “And he shall wave the sheaf before the LORD so that it may be accepted on your behalf…” So the priest takes the very first of the harvest and lifts it up before the LORD for the people. The timing is set too: “the priest is to wave it on the day after the Sabbath.” If I tried waving a sheaf with this mustache, there'd be grain on my ceiling.

Burning is in this passage, friend, but it belongs to the lamb. On the day the sheaf is waved, God says, “…you shall offer a year-old lamb without blemish as a burnt offering to the LORD…” The sheaf itself gets waved, not burned. Me, I only burn things by accident, and my cookies have the receipts.

Grinding sounds like the next step to me, since grain turns into flour somehow. But the text only says the priest waves the sheaf before the LORD. Fine flour does show up later, mixed with oil in the grain offering that goes with the lamb (v. 13).

Not yet, friend. God says, “You must not eat any bread or roasted or new grain until the very day you have brought this offering to your God.” The offering comes first, then the eating. Me, I can barely wait ten minutes for a batch to cool, so a rule like this would put my mustache to the test.

False is right. No bread, no roasted grain and no new grain “…until the very day you have brought this offering to your God.” And it isn't a one-time rule: “This is to be a permanent statute for the generations to come, wherever you live.”

Fifty. God says, “You shall count off fifty days until the day after the seventh Sabbath, and then present an offering of new grain to the LORD.” Seven full weeks is forty-nine days, and the day after makes fifty. The math checks out, even for a stamper.
Forty is a nice round number, friend, but it's not the one God gives here. He says to “…count off fifty days…” Seven full weeks, plus the day after the seventh Sabbath, lands you on fifty.

Seventy would be a very long countdown, friend. But God says fifty: “You shall count off fifty days until the day after the seventh Sabbath…” Seven weeks and then one more day, and the new grain is ready to bring.

Baked with leaven. The two loaves are “…each made from two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour, baked with leaven, as the firstfruits to the LORD.” That's different from the unleavened bread earlier in the chapter. Different feast, different loaves.

That's a natural guess after the Feast of Unleavened Bread, friend. But for these two loaves, the text says they're “…baked with leaven…” They come from the Israelites' own homes as the firstfruits to the LORD. Different feast, different instructions.

Honey isn't in this recipe, friend. The text says the loaves are made from two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour and “…baked with leaven…” They're brought from the Israelites' own homes as a wave offering. Honey's not on the list.

For the generations to come. God says, “This is to be a permanent statute wherever you live for the generations to come.” No end date is given. It's a day for the children's children and the ones after them.
The text never ties this day to a building project, friend. God says, “This is to be a permanent statute wherever you live for the generations to come.” There's no finish line in that sentence.
Seven years would be a short run, friend. God calls this day “…a permanent statute wherever you live for the generations to come.” Permanent means no countdown on this one.

explanations.answer: The poor and the foreign resident
explanations.explanation: The poor and the foreign resident. God says, “Leave them for the poor and the foreign resident. I am the LORD your God.” Leaving the edges and the gleanings is the whole instruction. Even I'd have to leave the last chocolate chip on the tray, and that would be a hard day.

The priests do get a share in this chapter, friend. The bread of the firstfruits and the two lambs are “…holy to the LORD for the priest.” (v. 20). But the edges and the gleanings are left for “…the poor and the foreign resident.”
No king shows up in this part of the chapter, friend. God says to leave the edges and gleanings “…for the poor and the foreign resident.” That's who the leftovers are for.

Trumpet blasts. God says the first day of the seventh month is “…a day of rest, a sacred assembly announced by trumpet blasts.” No group chat needed, just trumpets. Everybody within earshot gets the message.

Ruby, one of my cookie cutter kids, was the loudest voice in my kitchen, and she's a bell, so I had to look twice at this one. But the text says the day is “…a sacred assembly announced by trumpet blasts.” Bells didn't make the list, friend. Trumpets did.
Cymbals would definitely get everyone's attention, friend. But God says the day is “…a sacred assembly announced by trumpet blasts.” It's trumpets for this one.

Humble themselves. God says, “You shall hold a sacred assembly and humble yourselves, and present a food offering to the LORD.” It comes right alongside the assembly and the offering. This day is a different mood than a party, friend.

Joy gets its own feast later in the chapter, friend. For Tabernacles God says, “And you are to rejoice before the LORD your God for seven days.” (v. 40). For the Day of Atonement, the instruction is to “humble yourselves.”

Clothes never come up, friend. Along with the sacred assembly and the food offering, the instruction is “humble yourselves.” My apron has survived some serious chocolate chip disasters, so I'd have signed up for laundry day happily. But that's not what the text asks.

Not quite, friend. God says, “On this day you are not to do any work, for it is the Day of Atonement, when atonement is made for you before the LORD your God.” There's no after-assembly exception. He says it again: “You are not to do any work at all.”

False is right. “You are not to do any work at all.” God says, and He calls it “…a permanent statute for the generations to come, wherever you live.” The whole day is rest, assembly or no assembly. Not even a little catch-up.

explanations.answer: The evening of the ninth day
explanations.explanation: The evening of the ninth day. God says, “From the evening of the ninth day of the month until the following evening you are to keep your Sabbath.” So the rest starts the night before the tenth day. That's evening to evening.

The tenth day is the Day of Atonement, so sunrise is a fair guess. But God starts the clock earlier: “From the evening of the ninth day of the month until the following evening you are to keep your Sabbath.” The Sabbath begins the evening before.

Noon would be a late start, friend. God says, “From the evening of the ninth day of the month until the following evening you are to keep your Sabbath.” It runs evening to evening, starting the night before the tenth.

True, friend. The seven days finish, and then God adds one more: “On the eighth day you are to hold a sacred assembly and present a food offering to the LORD. It is a solemn assembly; you must not do any regular work.” Just when you think the feast is wrapping up, there's one more day. It's like finding one last cookie at the bottom of the box.

This one is true, friend. The feast runs seven days, and then comes one more. God says, “On the eighth day you are to hold a sacred assembly and present a food offering to the LORD. It is a solemn assembly; you must not do any regular work.”

Fruit and branches. God says, “On the first day you are to gather the fruit of majestic trees, the branches of palm trees, and the boughs of leafy trees and of willows of the brook.” That's quite a shopping list for one day. Palm branches, leafy boughs and willows, all in one pile.

Stones aren't on the list, friend. The text says to gather “…the fruit of majestic trees, the branches of palm trees, and the boughs of leafy trees and of willows of the brook.” Willows grow by the brook, but it's the branches God asks for.

Wool isn't mentioned here, friend. God tells Israel to gather fruit and branches: “…the fruit of majestic trees, the branches of palm trees, and the boughs of leafy trees and of willows of the brook.” It's all from trees.

Rejoice. God says, “And you are to rejoice before the LORD your God for seven days.” That's a different tone from the Day of Atonement, where the word was “humble yourselves.” A whole week of it, friend.
Mourning isn't the word, friend. For this feast God says, “And you are to rejoice before the LORD your God for seven days.” The harvest is in, and the instruction is rejoicing.

Fasting isn't in this verse, friend. God says, “And you are to rejoice before the LORD your God for seven days.” The harvest is gathered, and the word is rejoice. A fast with my bakery right next door? I'd last about four minutes.

explanations.answer: So later generations know God had Israel live in booths
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. God says it's “…so that your descendants may know that I made the Israelites dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt.” It's a yearly way for their descendants to know it. And He signs it: “I am the LORD your God.”

explanations.answer: So they can stay close to their fields at harvest
explanations.explanation: That sounds sensible, friend, but the text doesn't give that reason. God says the booths are “…so that your descendants may know that I made the Israelites dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt.” The reason is for their descendants to know.

explanations.answer: So their houses are free for travelers that week
explanations.explanation: Travelers don't come up here, friend. The reason God gives is “…so that your descendants may know that I made the Israelites dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt.” It's about remembering what God did.

Not quite, friend. The last verse says, “So Moses announced to the Israelites the appointed feasts of the LORD.” He announced them to the Israelites, not only to the priests. And all through the chapter, God keeps telling Moses to “Speak to the Israelites…”

False is right, friend. The last verse says, “So Moses announced to the Israelites the appointed feasts of the LORD.” God had told him to “Speak to the Israelites…” and the chapter ends with Moses announcing the feasts to them. This calendar was not a priests-only memo.
